title: Plate Tectonics and Volcanoes
seo_title: Geology 12: Plate Tectonics and Volcanoes Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
short_title: plate boundaries, volcanoes and mountain building
standard_text: Plate tectonic theory: plate boundaries and their features, mantle convection, volcanoes and magma types, mountain building, and the tectonic history of BC. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Geology 12)
meta_desc: Free Geology 12 worksheets (BC Curriculum): plate boundaries, volcanoes and mountain building. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Most volcanoes are at plate boundaries.
key_sub: Silica-rich magma is sticky and explosive.
body_html:
How to think about it

Plates move apart at divergent boundaries, collide at convergent boundaries and slide past at transform boundaries. Subduction zones make deep trenches, volcanic arcs and large earthquakes; continental collisions build mountain ranges.

Basaltic (low-silica) magma is runny and makes gentle shield volcanoes. Andesitic and rhyolitic (high-silica) magma is sticky and traps gas, making explosive stratovolcanoes such as Mount St. Helens. Hot spots, such as Hawaii, form volcanoes away from boundaries.

Example

Which magma makes explosive eruptions?

Sticky, gas-rich

Answer: high-silica magma

Example

What kind of boundary forms a mid-ocean ridge?

Plates move apart.

Answer: divergent

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all volcanoes erupt the same way.
  • Thinking hot spots are at plate boundaries.
  • Mixing up the lithosphere and the asthenosphere.

faq.q: Why are there volcanoes in BC's Garibaldi belt?
faq.a: The Juan de Fuca plate subducts and melts beneath North America.
A block of crust with its own geology that was added to a continent by plate motion; much of BC is made of terranes.

items.q: Which action best reduces the risk to people from volcanic eruptions?
c: clearing brush to make defensible space around homes
monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people
building codes that make structures flexible and strong
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: A tsunami crosses ocean 4000 m deep. Its speed is v = √(gd). How long does it take to travel 4000 km? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
Which action best reduces the risk to people from droughts?
c: water conservation and storing water in reservoirs
drainage and retaining walls on steep slopes
monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: How many times larger is the ground motion (wave amplitude) of a magnitude 7 earthquake than a magnitude 5 earthquake?
items.e: Each step of 1 is ×10 in amplitude: 10^(7 − 5) = 100 times.

items.q: Which action best reduces the risk to people from river floods?
c: ocean sensors linked to warning sirens
zoning that keeps homes off the floodplain
water conservation and storing water in reservoirs
drainage and retaining walls on steep slopes
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: At a seismic station the S-waves arrive 60 s after the P-waves. Using 8 km of distance for each second of lag, how far away is the epicentre?
items.e: 60 × 8 = 480 km. Three stations are needed to locate the epicentre.

items.q: At a seismic station the S-waves arrive 10 s after the P-waves. Using 8 km of distance for each second of lag, how far away is the epicentre?
items.e: 10 × 8 = 80 km. Three stations are needed to locate the epicentre.

items.q: A community plans monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people. Which hazard is this mainly meant to reduce?
items.e: Match the plan to the hazard.

items.q: About how many times more energy is released by a magnitude 9 earthquake than a magnitude 7 earthquake? (Each step of 1 is about 32 times the energy.)
How many times larger is the ground motion (wave amplitude) of a magnitude 6 earthquake than a magnitude 4 earthquake?
items.e: Each step of 1 is ×10 in amplitude: 10^(6 − 4) = 100 times.

items.q: Which is a way to reduce the risk of earthquake damage?
c: building codes that require flexible, reinforced structures
items.e: Planning and drills also help.

items.q: How many times larger is the ground motion (wave amplitude) of a magnitude 9.1 earthquake than a magnitude 6.5 earthquake?
items.e: Each step of 1 is ×10 in amplitude: 10^(9.1 − 6.5) = 398 times.

items.q: How many times larger is the ground motion (wave amplitude) of a magnitude 7 earthquake than a magnitude 5.6 earthquake?
items.e: Each step of 1 is ×10 in amplitude: 10^(7 − 5.6) = 25.1 times.

items.q: At a seismic station the S-waves arrive 40 s after the P-waves. Using 8 km of distance for each second of lag, how far away is the epicentre?
items.e: 40 × 8 = 320 km. Three stations are needed to locate the epicentre.

items.q: A tsunami crosses ocean 5000 m deep. Its speed is v = √(gd). How long does it take to travel 2000 km? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
Which action best reduces the risk to people from hurricanes?
c: zoning that keeps homes off the floodplain
monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people
ocean sensors linked to warning sirens
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: About how many times more energy is released by a magnitude 7 earthquake than a magnitude 4 earthquake? (Each step of 1 is about 32 times the energy.)
Which type of volcano has gentle slopes and runny basalt lava?
items.e: Hawaii's volcanoes are shield volcanoes.

items.q: How can a volcanic eruption cool the global climate?
c: sulfur dioxide forms sulfate aerosols in the stratosphere that reflect sunlight
ash adds heat to the air
items.e: Pinatubo (1991) cooled Earth by about 0.5 °C.

items.q: What can trigger a landslide?
c: heavy rain, earthquakes or removal of vegetation on steep slopes
items.e: Thredbo (1997) was a landslide disaster.

items.q: Seafloor spreads at 2 cm per year. About how old is rock 40 km from the ridge?
Emma finds seafloor rock 500 km from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that is 25 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100000 cm)
items.e: 500 km = 50000000 cm; ÷ 25 million years = 2 cm/yr.

items.q: How did Earth's layers form?
c: early Earth was hot enough to melt, so dense iron sank to form the core and lighter rock rose
they were all added by meteorites in order
the crust formed first and then the core
items.e: This separation is called differentiation.

items.q: Emma finds seafloor rock 25 km from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that is 1 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100000 cm)
items.e: 25 km = 2500000 cm; ÷ 1 million years = 2.5 cm/yr.

items.q: What forms where two oceanic plates move apart?
c: a mid-ocean ridge with new crust
items.e: Magma rises to fill the gap.

items.q: A plate moves away from a mid-ocean ridge at 3 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 40 million years ago? (100000 cm = 1 km)
Ava finds seafloor rock 100 km from the East Pacific Rise that is 2 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100000 cm)
items.e: 100 km = 10000000 cm; ÷ 2 million years = 5 cm/yr.

items.q: Which layer of Earth is liquid?
items.e: S-waves cannot travel through it.

items.q: How do we know the outer core is liquid?
c: S-waves (shear waves) do not travel through it, leaving an S-wave shadow zone
items.e: P-waves pass through but are refracted.

items.q: Ethan finds seafloor rock 4000 km from the East Pacific Rise that is 50 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100000 cm)
items.e: 4000 km = 400000000 cm; ÷ 50 million years = 8 cm/yr.

items.q: Which statement about the age of oceanic crust is correct?
c: it is older than most continental crust
it is youngest at mid-ocean ridges and gets older away from them
it is the same age everywhere
it is oldest at mid-ocean ridges
items.e: Oceanic crust is rarely older than about 200 million years.

items.q: What is the principle of superposition?
c: the youngest layers are at the bottom
all layers formed at the same time
in undisturbed sedimentary layers, the lowest layers are the oldest
items.e: It gives relative ages.

items.q: A plate moves away from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge at 1 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 10 million years ago? (100000 cm = 1 km)
A plate moves away from the East Pacific Rise at 6 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 10 million years ago? (100000 cm = 1 km)
Seafloor spreads at 6 cm per year. About how old is rock 1200 km from the ridge?
Which feature is most likely at a convergent boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
items.e: convergent (plates move together): volcanoes along the Andes.

items.q: What forms where an oceanic plate subducts beneath another plate?
c: a deep trench and a chain of volcanoes
items.e: The Pacific 'Ring of Fire' has many subduction zones.

items.q: Jayden finds seafloor rock 160 km from a mid-ocean ridge that is 4 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100000 cm)
items.e: 160 km = 16000000 cm; ÷ 4 million years = 4 cm/yr.

items.q: A plate moves away from the East Pacific Rise at 10 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 5 million years ago? (100000 cm = 1 km)
Which feature is most likely at a transform boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
items.e: transform (plates slide past each other): the San Andreas Fault.

items.q: A plate moves away from a mid-ocean ridge at 4 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 4 million years ago? (100000 cm = 1 km)
Seafloor spreads at 5 cm per year. About how old is rock 200 km from the ridge?
Evidence: Magnetic stripes on the seafloor are symmetric on both sides of the ridge. What does it support?
c: New crust forms at the ridge and spreads both ways.
The continents may once have been joined.
The rocks formed together before the continents split.
items.e: Many lines of evidence support plate tectonics.

items.q: Evidence: GPS stations show Hawaii moving about 7 cm per year toward Japan. What does it support?
c: The continents may once have been joined.
Antarctica was once near the equator.
items.e: Many lines of evidence support plate tectonics.

items.q: A plate moves away from the East Pacific Rise at 6 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 20 million years ago? (100000 cm = 1 km)
Evidence: The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces. What does it support?
c: The continents may once have been joined.
The rocks formed together before the continents split.
New crust forms at the ridge and spreads both ways.
items.e: Many lines of evidence support plate tectonics.

items.q: Evidence: The same fossil reptile, Mesosaurus, is found in South America and Africa. What does it support?
c: New crust forms at the ridge and spreads both ways.
Antarctica was once near the equator.
The southern continents were together near the South Pole.
items.e: Many lines of evidence support plate tectonics.

items.q: Two plates pull apart on land, as in East Africa. What feature forms?
c: a deep trench and a chain of volcanic mountains
a mid-ocean ridge with new crust
items.e: Divergent: ridges and rifts. Convergent: trenches, volcanoes, mountains. Transform: earthquakes.

items.q: A plate moves away from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge at 1 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 1 million years ago? (100000 cm = 1 km)
A plate moves away from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge at 2.5 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 2 million years ago? (100000 cm = 1 km)
One ocean plate sinks under another, as near Japan. What feature forms?
c: a trench and a curved chain of volcanic islands
a deep trench and a chain of volcanic mountains
items.e: Divergent: ridges and rifts. Convergent: trenches, volcanoes, mountains. Transform: earthquakes.

items.q: Hana finds seafloor rock 600 km from the East Pacific Rise that is 10 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100000 cm)
items.e: 600 km = 60000000 cm; ÷ 10 million years = 6 cm/yr.

items.q: Which boundary makes a rift valley?
c: Two plates slide past each other, as at the San Andreas Fault
An ocean plate sinks under a continent, as off South America
Two plates pull apart on land, as in East Africa
Two plates pull apart under the ocean
items.e: Match the motion to the feature.

items.q: Which evidence best supports this idea: “The continents may once have been joined.”
c: Rock layers and mountain belts match across the Atlantic Ocean.
The same fossil reptile, Mesosaurus, is found in South America and Africa.
The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces.
GPS stations show Hawaii moving about 7 cm per year toward Japan.
items.e: Match the evidence.

items.q: Evidence: Coal from tropical swamps is found in Antarctica. What does it support?
c: The southern continents were together near the South Pole.
Antarctica was once near the equator.
items.e: Many lines of evidence support plate tectonics.

items.q: Aiden finds seafloor rock 640 km from the East Pacific Rise that is 8 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100000 cm)
items.e: 640 km = 64000000 cm; ÷ 8 million years = 8 cm/yr.

items.q: A plate moves away from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge at 2 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 4 million years ago? (100000 cm = 1 km)
Evidence: Rock layers and mountain belts match across the Atlantic Ocean. What does it support?
c: The rocks formed together before the continents split.
The southern continents were together near the South Pole.
New crust forms at the ridge and spreads both ways.
items.e: Many lines of evidence support plate tectonics.

items.q: Seafloor spreads at 2 cm per year. About how old is rock 100 km from the ridge?
Two plates slide past each other, as at the San Andreas Fault. What feature forms?
c: a trench and a curved chain of volcanic islands
very high folded mountains like the Himalayas
items.e: Divergent: ridges and rifts. Convergent: trenches, volcanoes, mountains. Transform: earthquakes.

items.q: A P wave travels 480 km at 8 km/s through the crust and upper mantle. How long does it take?
What happens to the solar radiation that reaches Earth?
c: it all passes back into space unchanged
some is reflected, some is absorbed by the atmosphere and most is absorbed by the surface
it is all absorbed by the Moon
items.e: Absorbed energy is later emitted as infrared.

items.q: Why does the Equator receive more solar energy per square metre than the poles?
c: sunlight hits it more directly, so the energy is spread over a smaller area
it is closer to the Sun
items.e: At the poles the same beam is spread out.

items.q: What is Earth's average albedo?
items.e: About 30% of sunlight is reflected.

items.q: A P wave travels 1800 km at 8 km/s through the crust and upper mantle. How long does it take?
Which type of radiation does Earth's surface mainly emit?
items.e: Cooler objects emit longer wavelengths.

items.q: Seafloor spreads at 5 cm per year. About how old is rock 2000 km from the ridge?
Seafloor spreads at 6 cm per year. About how old is rock 3000 km from the ridge?
Seafloor spreads at 4 cm per year. About how old is rock 320 km from the ridge?
What is latent heat's role in weather?
c: energy taken up in evaporation is released when water vapour condenses in clouds, powering storms
items.e: Tropical cyclones are fuelled by latent heat.

items.q: Which energy source drives the water cycle?
items.e: Evaporation needs energy.

items.q: How does the greenhouse effect work?
c: greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation from Earth's surface and re-emit some back down
items.e: Without it Earth would average about −18 °C.

items.q: Liam finds seafloor rock 1000 km from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that is 50 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100000 cm)
items.e: 1000 km = 100000000 cm; ÷ 50 million years = 2 cm/yr.

items.q: Why is Earth's internal heat still flowing out after 4.5 billion years?
c: radioactive isotopes keep producing heat, and the deep interior holds heat from Earth's formation
items.e: Uranium-238 has a half-life of 4.5 billion years.

items.q: A P wave travels 600 km at 8 km/s through the crust and upper mantle. How long does it take?

Hana models convection by heating water with food colouring. What does the moving colour represent?
items.e: Warm material rises and cool material sinks.

items.q: Which layer of Earth is the solid centre of iron and nickel?
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms mid-ocean ridges?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Which layer of Earth is the thin, solid outer layer we live on?
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: What is Earth's mantle like?
c: the thick layer of hot rock that flows very slowly
the thin, solid outer layer we live on
the layer of liquid iron and nickel
the solid centre of iron and nickel
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a divergent boundary?
c: the Alpine Fault in New Zealand
a flat desert in the middle of a plate
items.e: divergent (plates move apart): rift valleys in East Africa.

items.q: Chloe measures the distance between two GPS stations across a boundary: it grows 3 cm each year. What kind of boundary is it?
items.e: Moving apart means divergent.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a transform boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
the Alpine Fault in New Zealand
items.e: transform (plates slide past each other): the Alpine Fault in New Zealand.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a transform boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
sudden earthquakes along a fault line
fold mountains such as the Himalayas
items.e: transform (plates slide past each other): sudden earthquakes along a fault line.

items.q: What is Earth's outer core like?
c: the layer of liquid iron and nickel
the thin, solid outer layer we live on
the solid centre of iron and nickel
the thick layer of hot rock that flows very slowly
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a convergent boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
items.e: convergent (plates move together): deep ocean trenches.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms sudden earthquakes along a fault line?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Which layer of Earth is the layer of liquid iron and nickel?
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms the Southern Alps of New Zealand pushing up?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Kai uses a jigsaw of continents to show Gondwana. What is a limitation of his model?
c: Coastlines have changed, and the real fit uses the edges of the continental shelves.
It shows plates moving too slowly.
items.e: Models simplify reality.

items.q: Why do scientists keep revising the theory of plate tectonics?
c: New evidence from GPS, sea-floor mapping and earthquakes improves it.
items.e: Scientific theories develop with new evidence.

items.q: What is Earth's crust like?
c: the thin, solid outer layer we live on
the thick layer of hot rock that flows very slowly
the solid centre of iron and nickel
the layer of liquid iron and nickel
items.e: From outside in: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

items.q: Arjun plots earthquakes on a world map. Where are most of them?
items.e: The pattern shows where plates meet.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a convergent boundary?
c: sudden earthquakes along a fault line
fold mountains such as the Himalayas
a flat desert in the middle of a plate
items.e: convergent (plates move together): fold mountains such as the Himalayas.

items.q: What is Earth's inner core like?
c: the layer of liquid iron and nickel
the solid centre of iron and nickel
the thin, solid outer layer we live on
the thick layer of hot rock that flows very slowly
